summary: Discusses how MIME affects Internet mail gateways. MIME was designed so mail transport did not need changes, but there are ways transport systems may want to take advantage of it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Mail gateways are like post office sorting stations. This paper explains what they need to know about MIME envelopes so they handle fancy messages properly.

questions: how can mail gateways handle rejected mime messages
how does mime help with large email attachments
subtitle: How mail gateways can take advantage of MIME to improve service

tldr.problem: Internet mail gateways need to handle non-text messages, manage size limitations, and preserve message format when making transformations. Without standard approaches, rejected messages become hard to read and messages get lost.
tldr.mechanism: MIME provides a standardized format for encapsulating messages, fragmenting large ones, and referencing external data. Gateways can use these features to handle rejection, size constraints, and format optimization while keeping the message semantics intact.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems can transparently handle complex messages and offer better service to users without changing the base transport system, which was never required to understand MIME.

today: RFC 1344 is Informational and remains a reference for how mail systems can make use of MIME at the gateway level. The mechanisms described—message preservation, fragmentation, external references, and format conversion—are still relevant to email gateway design.

sections.title: Why MIME Matters to Mail Gateways
sections.content:
MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) was designed so that mail transport systems did not need to change to support richer message content. However, this does not mean transport systems should ignore MIME. The RFC shows several practical ways that mail gateways—systems that exchange mail between different mail environments—can take advantage of MIME to provide better service.

A critical distinction is made between mail transport services, which move messages within a single mail network, and gateways, which translate between different systems. Unlike transport services, which should never alter a message, gateways often must modify messages to cross boundaries. MIME makes this modification safe and reversible.
sections.eli5: MIME is like an instruction sheet on the envelope. Mail carriers don't need to read it, but sorting offices can use it to do their job better without breaking the mail inside.

sections.title: Preserving Rejected Messages with MIME
sections.content:
One frequent problem in mail systems is the need to reject a message—because it is undeliverable, too large, or does not conform to the destination's requirements. In the past, rejected messages were returned as plain text, which meant that if the original message contained an image or audio, the user would see corrupted binary data instead of the original content.

MIME solves this with the multipart/mixed message type. A rejection notice becomes a two-part message: a text part explaining the reason for rejection, followed by a message/rfc822 part that encapsulates the entire original message, including all its headers and any non-text content. The gateway does not need to understand the rejected message's structure; it simply wraps it intact. A MIME-aware mail reader at the receiving end can display both the rejection reason and the original message in its correct form.
sections.eli5: Instead of throwing away the package and leaving just a note, the post office can put the whole unopened package in a new envelope with a note explaining why it came back.

sections.title: Managing Large Messages
sections.content:
As MIME allows very large attachments such as images and audio, size limitations become a real problem. Gateways that connect to systems with strict size caps would often reject large messages unnecessarily. MIME provides two mechanisms: message/partial for fragmenting large messages, and message/external-body for avoiding large transfers altogether.

The message/partial type allows a single message to be automatically split into numbered fragments, each small enough to pass through the gateway. The receiving system reassembles them transparently, or the fragments can be reassembled by a user agent. Similarly, message/external-body lets the message body be stored on an FTP server instead of transmitted in the email itself. The message contains just the location information needed to fetch it later. A gateway might transform an external-body reference into actual data when crossing a slow boundary, or copy the data to a closer FTP server and update the reference, optimizing bandwidth and storage.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending a huge box, the post office can break it into smaller boxes or put a note saying where to pick up the package from a local warehouse.

sections.title: Format Conversion and Robust Encoding
sections.content:
MIME currently defines two image formats: image/gif and image/jpeg. GIF is more convenient for users and displays quickly on many systems, while JPEG is much more compact and reduces bandwidth. A gateway can intelligently convert between these formats: a GIF intended for long-haul delivery might be converted to JPEG for efficiency, while JPEG arriving at a system with plenty of storage might be converted to GIF for user convenience.

Additionally, when a message will cross a gateway to a system using a different character set (such as ASCII-to-EBCDIC), a gateway can apply MIME Content-Transfer-Encoding (base64 or quoted-printable) to ensure the data survives without loss. The RFC strongly recommends adding a Received header field to document any conversion performed, so users understand what changed.
sections.eli5: The post office can turn a big photo into a smaller one for slow links, or protect fragile text by wrapping it so it doesn't get damaged crossing different mail systems.

sections.title: User Control and Design Principles
sections.content:
Because gateways may perform major transformations on messages, some users will object. The RFC suggests that gateways allow users to control transformations via a Content-Conversion header field: a sender can set it to prohibited to forbid conversions, or permitted to allow them. However, the RFC notes that most gateways will assume conversions are permitted by default.

Throughout the memo, the key principle is that mail transport systems should remain conservative. Only gateways—systems that inherently modify messages—should perform the transformations described here. The overall goal is to let gateways provide better service to MIME users without breaking compatibility with systems that ignore MIME entirely.
sections.eli5: Users can add a label saying 'do not change this' or 'you can improve this.' The post office respects that, so you stay in control.

references.text: Borenstein, N., and N. Freed, "MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions): Mechanisms for Specifying and Describing the Format of Internet Message Bodies", RFC 1341, June 1992.
